title: Convergence of quasi-Newton matrices generated by the symmetric rank one update
contribution: Extends the quadratic-case exact-Hessian property of SR1 to general smooth functions: under uniformly linearly independent steps, SR1 matrices converge to the true Hessian at the limit point with an error proportional to the distance of recent iterates from it, confirmed numerically against BFGS, DFP and PSB.
problem_entry: Anomaly in the authors' own testing paper (CGT 1988 Math. Comp.): SR1 in a trust region beat BFGS, possibly because its matrices approximate the Hessian better; plus the case for indefinite updates (nonconvexity, constraints, sparsity) (pp. 5-6).
key_idea: SR1's hereditary secant property survives for nonquadratic f with secant errors growing only geometrically in the number of later updates times the iterate spread; a deliberately broad algorithm model (step unspecified, skip rule (17)) makes the theorem cover line-search, trust-region and partitioned-update methods (pp. 6-7, 9-10).
assumptions: f C^2 with Lipschitz Hessian, x_k -> x* (not necessarily stationary), SR1 skip rule |r^T s| >= c1||r|| ||s||, and uniformly linearly independent normalized steps sigma_min(S_k) >= c3 (AS.4), admitted to be strong with named failure modes; no line search, no positive definiteness (pp. 7-8, 12-13).
proof_devices: mean-value averaged Hessian y_l = Hbar_l s_l with Hbar_l = int_0^1 H(x_l + t s_l) dt (p. 10)
induction on updates since a secant pair was created, growth factor (2/c1 + 1)^{i-j-2} times iterate diameter eta_{i,j} (Lemma 1, pp. 9-10)
rate transfer: linear convergence of x_k gives ||B_{k+m+1} - H*|| <= c7 ||x_k - x*|| (Corollary 3, pp. 11-12)
computable bound c8 kappa(S*_k) eps_k in terms of the condition number of the last n normalized steps (Corollary 4, p. 12)
experiments: Quartic test functions with conditioning knob H = R D R^T (eigenvalues 1 to 2^-nu), seeds and RNG recurrence published; extended precision on CRAY X-MP; artificial sequences of prescribed rate, trust-region and line-search trajectories; entrywise Hessian error printed beside eps_k and kappa(S*_k); cost counted in gradient evaluations; SR1 errors 1e-9 to 1e-17 vs about 1e-3 to 1e-4 for BFGS/DFP/PSB; n = 3 and 10 only (pp. 13-19, 21).
positioning: Continues the authors' own [1],[2]; surveys Fiacco-McCormick, Powell (PSB), Ge-Powell (DFP/BFGS) and Schuller (BFGS) by their assumptions, credits Ge-Powell for not needing AS.4, and claims weaker assumptions than Schuller though only for SR1 (pp. 8-9, 12).
writing: Modest contribution framing ('clarify this suggestion'), roadmap, broad algorithm plus numbered justifying comments, assumption with evidence and failure modes, plain-language payoff after each result, candid 'very gross' constants, hedged conclusion ('throws some light') (pp. 6-8, 12, 20).
limits_future: AS.4 strong with named failure modes; bounds gross; only partly explains the SR1-vs-BFGS gap; future: analysis without AS.4, judged very difficult (pp. 8, 12, 20).

method_links.note: Triad run in reverse: the testing paper (CGT 1988 Math. Comp.) produced an unexplained result, the theorem follows, and new experiments check the theorem's predicted constant.
Step 1 (algorithm as a framework): the step s_k is left unspecified so the theorem covers line-search, trust-region and partitioned-update methods; also Research Taste mark 2.

Pre-DFO precursor: model (Hessian approximation) accuracy is tied to a geometric condition on sample directions (sigma_min(S_k), kappa(S*_k)), but geometry is assumed, not enforced by an improvement step; failure modes are named.
Partial: cost counted in gradient evaluations (ng); reproducible generator with published RNG recurrence; all updates and sequence types reported, including failures within budget.
Weak: indefinite updates motivated by large-scale sparsity; partitioned updating for partially separable functions is one reason the step is left free.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: An unexplained numerical result from the authors' own testing paper (SR1 beats BFGS in a trust region) becomes the next paper's theorem, with a hedged statement of how much it explains.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: experiments aimed at the theorem's predicted quantity
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Tables print eps_k and kappa(S*_k) beside the observed Hessian error so the constant c8 (about 0.1) can be read off.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: assumption calibrated on own run data, with failure modes
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: AS.4 justified by sigma_min > 1e-4 observed in the earlier tests, then two concrete failure mechanisms are given.

transferable: Mine your previous experimental paper for a result you cannot explain and make its explanation the next paper (pp. 5-6).
Support a strong assumption with a statistic measured in your own earlier runs, then list the mechanisms that break it (p. 8).
Lift error bounds along n well-spread directions to a matrix bound with ||A|| <= ||A S|| / sigma_min(S) (p. 11).
Write y_l = Hbar_l s_l with the averaged Hessian so Lipschitz continuity turns Hessian differences into iterate distances (pp. 10-11).
State a corollary whose bound is computable from a run and print that quantity next to the observed error in the tables (pp. 12, 15-19).
Drive the component under study with synthetic iterate sequences of prescribed rate before using real optimizer trajectories (pp. 14-19).
Build test problems with one conditioning parameter (H = R D R^T) and publish the random-number recurrence (pp. 13-14, 21).
coauthors: N. I. M. Gould, Ph. L. Toint

quotes.text: Somewhat surprisingly, the traditional supremacy of the BFGS update is questioned by these numerical experiments
Thus we obtain the quite interesting result that, the faster the convergence of {xk} to x∗, the faster the convergence of {Bk} to H(x∗)!

title: CUTE: Constrained and unconstrained testing environment
contribution: Publishes the LANCELOT-era testing apparatus as a stand-alone, solver-agnostic environment: a classified collection of 738 SIF test problems, database and selection tools, a SIF decoder with derivative evaluation tools, and interfaces to ten external solvers plus MATLAB.
problem_entry: The developers' own testing burden while building LANCELOT (obtain, specify, manage and compare), plus the lack of consensus on a problem-algorithm interface; posed as a new user's four successive questions (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Decouple problems from solvers: one structured input format (SIF, group partial separability) plus decoder, gather-style evaluation API in several derivative formats, a compact classification string with query tools, and thin template-based solver interfaces (pp. 8-23).
assumptions: Bound-constrained or generally constrained problems with smooth, group partially separable f and c_i (single group per constraint); irregular problems admitted and flagged; UNIX/C-shell bias acknowledged; no noise model (pp. 2, 8, 11, 21-22).
experiments: none (one illustrative UNCMIN run on MOREBV reporting evaluation counts, p. 16-17; solver results deferred to LANCELOT reports with nearly twenty thousand runs, p. 5)
positioning: In the spirit of Buckley (1992); inherits the Hock-Schittkowski/Bus classification; absorbs the Argonne, Hock-Schittkowski, Buckley, Minpack-2 and other collections by name; describes rival solvers neutrally; only comparative remark favours LANCELOT's structure exploitation (pp. 3-5, 14-16).
writing: Manual-like, low hedging; sections follow the user's question sequence; worked terminal sessions with real output; candid scope limits; conclusion lists six purposes and asks for user experience (pp. 2-3, 12-17, 25, 35-39).
limits_future: Classification deliberately limited (finer constraint, structural and solution information planned after user feedback, compatibly); no consensus interface; external solvers obtained separately; growth via licensed users; no performance-reporting methodology or noisy variants (not stated by authors) (pp. 3-5, 9, 25).

method_links.note: Primary practice source: the test bed is a published, public, classified, extensible, solver-agnostic product, with interfaces to rival-school codes such as COBYLA, NPSOL and VF13.

No noisy variants or noise model; the real-application tier exists only as metadata (origin letters A/M/R and application tables), consistent with the SKILL.md limitation that the 1990s CUTE style predates data profiles.
CUTE is the test leg of the LANCELOT triad: facilities built with LANCELOT, companion reports with about 20,000 option runs.
SIF, decoder and collection come from LANCELOT and are released for general use.
Structure built into the format: group partial separability as the input model; classification records sum-of-squares objectives and the degree of analytic derivatives supplied.
Weak: problems reach the authors through users, since the LANCELOT licence requires most users to submit typical problems (software users rather than industrial partners).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Compact classification string XXXr-XX-n-m for every problem plus select/classify/classall tools, allowing selection of all problems of a class.
One problem format, a decoder, gather-style evaluation tools in dense/coordinate/finite-element formats, and a template driver per solver.
The LANCELOT licence requires most users to submit typical problems, so the collection should become more user-oriented.

transferable: Give every benchmark problem a fixed-format class string (objective type, constraint type, smoothness, analytic derivative degree, origin, n, m) and ship a query tool; select test subsets by class, not by hand (pp. 8-10, 35-39).
Record each problem's origin (academic, modelling, real application) as metadata so results can be split into tiers (p. 8).
Put one evaluation API in front of all solvers (f, gradient, dense/coordinate/element Hessians, Hv products) with a template driver for adding a solver (pp. 17-23).
Ship one small smoke-test problem per interfaced solver to check installations before benchmarking (Table 4, p. 18).
Order an infrastructure paper by the user's questions and include a verbatim session transcript (pp. 3, 35-39).
Delay extending a shared classification until users give feedback, and commit to backward compatibility (p. 9).
coauthors: I. Bongartz, N. I. M. Gould, Ph. L. Toint

quotes.text: Moreover, not only can one assume that the collection will grow steadily, but because of the LANCELOT licensing agreement, which requires the submission of typical problems by most users of the package, the new problems are likely to be even more user-oriented than the present ones.
The only way to really judge the effectiveness of the environment is for the reader to use it.
